title: The month of Vaisakh
hookLine: in Vaisakh, how can the separated be patient (Barah Maha, ang 133)

lines: A HARD MONTH TO BE ALONE.
cards: Vaisakh is harvest month in Punjab, April into May. The wheat is cut and threshed, the grain goes to market, and for a farming family it's a well-fed, busy, crowded time. Fairs come to the villages.
Vaisakhi, the festival, falls in this month, and for Sikhs it carries the memory of the Vaisakhi when Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa. Everyone is home, celebrating.
And in the folk songs, that's what makes it a hard month to be the one whose beloved is missing.

teach.h: HOW CAN THE SEPARATED BE PATIENT?
teach.b: The Vaisakh stanza on ang 133 opens with a question. In paraphrase: in Vaisakh, how can the brides be patient, the ones separated from love? Dheeran, patience, steadiness.
How do you hold steady when everyone around you is with the one they love? Then Guru Arjan names why she's alone.

teach.h: CLINGING TO MAYA, FORGETTING THE FRIEND.
teach.b: She has forgotten the Lord, the true Friend, and clung to maya, the world's deceptive glitter. And he names what she clings to: sons, wife, wealth, none of which go along with you at the end. Only the One is imperishable.
Entangled in false busy-ness, the whole world is wearing itself out. Notice the timing. The grain is in.

The money's coming. Guru Arjan isn't against any of that; Sikhs are householders, and earning honestly is part of the path. But the fullest month of the year is also an easy month to forget the One entirely.
Plenty can be loud. Then the stanza turns.

teach.h: BEAUTIFUL WHEN THE LORD IS MET.
teach.b: Vaisakh becomes beautiful, it says, when a holy person brings you to meet the Lord. The same harvest, festival and crowded house become lovely once the missing one is found. So the ache isn't the end.

Longing is a kind of compass needle: it points to what's missing, and a person who never felt it might never look. Vaisakh is the month of having almost everything, and the stanza asks gently what the almost is.

how: On the sangrand of Vaisakh, gurdwaras that keep the day read the Vaisakh stanza of the Barah Maha, and Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi in this month, remembering the founding of the Khalsa.

o: the planting month, when fields are sown
the harvest month, when longing is sharpest
a single festival day honoring the Khalsa

games.q: the month of Vaisakh — tap the pairs.

s: the Vaisakh stanza condemns the harvest and earning
Sikhs are householders; the stanza warns that plenty can make us forget.
the stanza opens by asking how the separated can be patient
dheeran: how can they hold steady?
the stanza says sons, wife and wealth go with you at the end
none of them go along; only the One is imperishable.

games.q: it's Vaisakh, the grain is in, the house is full, and still you feel something missing. what does the stanza say makes the month beautiful?
o: meeting the Lord, through a holy person.
games.why: Vaisakh becomes beautiful, the stanza says, when a holy person brings you to meet the Lord. the longing is the door.

practice: Let one person come to mind whose absence you feel, someone living and reachable you haven't spoken to in too long, and picture their voice. Feel the missing plainly, the way the stanza does, and hold their face for a few breaths.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them.

wordCard.voice: Vaisakh. Harvest and festival, when the separated bride can't hold steady, and the month becomes beautiful only when the Beloved is met.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: in Vaisakh, the harvest month; the stanza's first word.

carryVoice: Your line: vaisakh: longing. The ache is a door, not the end. On to the heat tomorrow.

sources.ref: Barah Maha, Majh M5, Vaisakh stanza, Ang 133–134
